blocks.text: II. The second passage on the hasida is Iob. XXXIX, 16. (var. 13.), where the ostrich is compared with the hasida, that is, with the stork, with respect to wing and plumage. For the Sacred Writer says: The wing of ostriches exults, truly a wing as of the stork, [III, 89] and plumage, that is, of the same colour as it. That this clause must be rendered so, we have shown with many arguments ^{c)} in the treatise On the ostrich; and the ostrich is rightly compared in this respect with the stork, because of the mixture of black with white in the colour of their feathers. Hence Scaliger, Against Cardano, Exercise 230: All (ostriches) are marked with dark and white, as many African merchants told me; and so that I might understand it better, they compared it to the colour of the stork. Marmol, on the ostrich, in his Africa, book 1, chapter 23: En las alas, y en la cola tiene grandes plumas negras, y blancas, comelas de cigueña, that is, On the wings and on the tail it has large black and white feathers, like the feathers of the stork. For there is no one who does not know that storks are marked with these colours. Hence Albertus: The stork has black wings, and a white tail and other parts. And Turner: It is a bird of a size between the crane and the heron, marked with white and black feathers. Nor does the Greek name of the stork, πελαργὸς [pelargos], come from anywhere else; it is observed to be compounded of two opposites, namely black and white. For πελὸν [pelon] means τὸ μέλαν [to melan], καὶ ἀργὸν τὸ λευκόν [kai argon to leukon]. See Suidas, the Etymologicum and Eustathius on Iliad λ΄ [11]. From this mixture of colours the γυπαίετος [gypaietos], the vulture-eagle, is called ὀρειπέλαργος [oreipelargos], that is, mountain stork, and περκνόπτερος [perknopteros], that is, having black wings. See Aristotle, History, book 9, chapter 32, and Pliny, book 10, chapter 3. And in Lycophron the πελαργοχρῶτες, αἱ Φαλακραίαι κόραι [pelargochrōtes, hai Phalakraiai korai], Phalacraean daughters having the colour of storks, are the ships of the Greeks built at Phalacra, a promontory of Ida, [col. 330] and having a mixed τὸ πελὸν καὶ τὸ ἀργὸν χρῶμα [to pelon kai to argon chrōma], black and white colour ^{(3)}.

III. The third passage on the hasida is Psal. CIV, 17. (var. CIII, 19.) חסידה ברושים ביתה, The firs are the house of the hasida. Here house stands for nest, as in Psalm. [III, 90] LXXXIV, 4. (var. LXXXIII, 3.) Even the sparrow has found בית קן, a nest for itself. So in the second book of the Georgics,
And he tears up the ancient homes of the birds together with the lowest roots. — —
